newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar slides after Reserve Bank statement.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar slides after Reserve Bank statement.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar slid 35 basis points in late Thursday morning trading after the Reserve Bank issued a statement saying monetary conditions had tightened more than necessary.
At 11.30 a.m. (2230 GMT) the Kiwi dollar was trading at US$0.7063/70 compared with around 71 U.S. cents in early trading. The Trade-Weighted Index fell to 67.41 from 67.75.
Dealers said everyone knew that conditions were too tight but a statement from the Reserve Bank still came as something of a surprise.
"They obviously do want the currency down," a dealer said.

David Archer, Chief Manager of the Reserve Bank's Financial Markets Department, said: "The sharp exchange rate appreciation that we have seen in recent days has been accompanied by a relatively small drop in interest rates, leading to a marked tightening in overall monetary conditions."

He said while the bank had expressed concern about too rapid an easing in monetary conditions following the surprisingly low inflation result for the September quarter, it could see no particular policy requirement for monetary conditions to have firmed as much as has occurred in recent days.

Archer said that in order to keep overall monetary conditions consistent with price stability, it seemed the bank would have to accept rather less interest rate pressure and rather more exchange rate pressure than might be ideal.
Dealers said Kiwi buyers were scarce and more sellers were coming into the market.
"Anyone who wants to buy it is probably a lot lower," a dealer said.
He said it appeared the bank was bringing its easing of monetary conditions forward after some further comfirmation of easing inflation pressures since the positive September quarter CPI data.
"Everyone had been expecting an easing some time in December and they may well have looked at the data available to them and said 'we can bring that forward.'
"I don't think they are in any way backing down on their inflationary stance," the dealer said.
